title: Testosterone for menopause: The treatment is rising in popularity, but does it work?
summary: Women are using testosterone in the hope that it will treat their menopause symptoms, but little evidence supports the approach, experts say.
body: If you're approaching menopause, you are likely being bombarded by online ads for treatments promising relief for everything from hot flashes to brain fog. Some of these therapies have been approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and have strong evidence to support them — but one hormone-based treatment that's gaining in popularity has much less science to back its use for menopause. More doctors are writing their menopausal patients prescriptions for testosterone therapy. A 2026 study conducted in the U.S. recorded over 90,000 off-label prescriptions for testosterone to women in 2025, mainly among women ages 45 to 64 and those with diagnoses of menopause. This marked a 58.7% increase from 2024. These prescriptions are "off-label" because the FDA has not yet approved testosterone as a treatment for menopause, perimenopause (the transition into menopause) or postmenopause (the time period afterward). So, does scientific evidence support the use of testosterone to alleviate menopause symptoms? Or is it too soon to say? title: Teenager's rare autoimmune disorder caused her to hallucinate a flying green dinosaur
summary: Doctors ran many tests to uncover the cause of a teen girl's auditory and visual hallucinations.
body: The patient: A 16-year-old girl in California The symptoms: The teenager was referred to an emergency department because she was having hallucinations, including seeing a flying green dinosaur and hearing voices telling her to hurt others. She also had a sense that she was being followed. In the emergency room, she was trembling and sweating and had a racing pulse and shallow, fast breathing. She did not have a fever, although she did have one at the hospital that had referred her. During her conversations with ER clinicians, the teen reacted to the vision of the dinosaur as though the creature were present in the room. She reported that she had experienced these hallucinations since seventh grade,‬ so for about four years. While her parents countered that she hadn’t exhibited psychotic symptoms until 48 hours before they arrived in the ER, they noted that her interest in school and extracurriculars had waned over the past month. What happened next: Because of the patient's abnormal vital signs, the ER doctors suspected that her hallucinations might be secondary to some physical ailment, such as trauma to the brain, they wrote in a case report . title: Flu season is kicking off early — are you getting a vaccine?
summary: New data reveals that flu season is off to an early start in several Western states. Live Science wants to know if you have already gotten the flu vaccine or plan to do so this year.
body: Flu season in the U.S. typically starts around late October or early November and peaks between December and February. But new data reveals that the current flu season is starting slightly earlier than normal . According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) , around 3.4% of respiratory samples tested for flu came back positive for the week of Sept. 26. That's around seven times the rate compared with the same week in 2025 . title: 'October is the ideal time to get vaccinated': Flu season is kicking off early, experts say
summary: Flu tests are coming back positive at higher rates than is typical for early fall in several Western states, data suggests.
body: Flu season is off to an early start in some parts of the U.S., data shows. In a typical year, U.S. flu activity starts building in late fall — typically in October or November — and peaks between December and February. This year, flu activity is currently low but rising nationwide: During the week ending Sept. 26, 3.4% of respiratory samples tested by clinical labs were positive for flu, according to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) data . That's about seven times the rate that was seen at the same point last year. About 0.5% of samples tested positive during the week ending Sept. 27, 2025. "This particular year, it appears to be starting early — like right now," Dr. William Schaffner , a professor of preventive medicine and infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health in Tennessee, told Live Science. Patients at clinics in his area are already testing positive for flu, he said. The early uptick in flu is mostly unfolding in Western states, including Washington, California and Arizona .
